headline.en_html: President Trump Starts Asia Trip by Shrugging Off U.S. Concerns: ‘It’s Fine’
headline.zh: 川总启程出访亚洲，对国内的种种担忧一概耸肩不理：“没事。”

paragraphs.en_html: President Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday, at the tail end of a diplomatic summit in which world leaders had arranged to hold part of the gathering at his hotel. His agenda was supposed to be about inking trade deals and embracing regional partnerships, but several problems from home had followed him overseas.

He was pelted with questions. He seemed to meet each with a shrug. Did he have any worries about the aviation-system meltdown afflicting travelers across the United States, or a technological outage affecting several large banking systems? “It’s life,” Mr. Trump said. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.” What about news reports, so far unconfirmed by the Trump administration, that Iran may be thinking about how to unleash a dirty bomb in Washington? Was an attack on American soil imminent? “I hope it’s not,” Mr. Trump said, not exactly the voice of reassurance. “But we take it very seriously. Because they happen to be crazy.”

Mr. Trump’s visit to Manila amounted to a layover. When he arrived, he trudged off the plane like all weary long-haul travelers do, and slowly made his way down the stairs of Air Force One. Mr. Trump was then whisked to his hotel, where several world leaders had gathered to bring the diplomatic summit to his doorstep.

Mr. Trump’s trip was planned before the midterm elections, but few Republicans, including Mr. Trump, had predicted them to be a near complete wipeout of the president’s handpicked candidates. His appearance in Asia, two weeks after the election, is in keeping with a long tradition of global trips taken by presidents hoping to divert attention from a damaging domestic story by flexing American power abroad.

In November 1994, days after Republicans took control of Congress for the first time in decades, President Bill Clinton departed for the Philippines. In 2010, after Democrats lost 63 House seats, President Barack Obama traveled through India, Indonesia, South Korea, Japan and Portugal. Mr. Trump even did it in his first term, jetting to France after Republicans lost control of the House in 2018.

This time, there was little of substance on Mr. Trump’s schedule aside from signing a trade deal between the United States and Thailand. In the end, not even the trade deal materialized, with the president saying that it would be finished in the coming weeks. “I look forward to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks,” Mr. Trump said. “Our staff is working on it very diligently, and it’ll be done. But the concept of what we have will be really very permanent, and we’re just about there.” He signed something anyway, even in the absence of a deal, under the theory that no favorable photo should go unsnapped.

Before ending his day, Mr. Trump delivered remarks at a dinner of ASEAN leaders, and praised his host, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines. “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Mr. Trump said. “I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”

On Wednesday, Mr. Trump will stay in Manila long enough to have lunch at Malacañang Palace and a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos before departing for Shenzhen. In China, Mr. Trump needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

Also lingering over Mr. Trump’s trip to Asia is the fallout from the resignation of Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, after revelations he had engaged in extramarital affairs. Mr. Huang has been influential in shaping the president’s views about technological competition with China, and made the argument that keeping China dependent on American-made semiconductor chips and technology could help maintain U.S. dominance over Beijing.

Before leaving for Manila, Mr. Trump did not seem concerned about the scandal that has rocked a corporate juggernaut that is critical to the A.I. industry. His usual retort when asked about spying is that everyone does it, and he did not seem especially perturbed. If he was, he would not show it. “You know, we’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” Mr. Trump said.
